title: Mobile phone ownership, social media use, and substance use at ages 11-13 in the ABCD study
authors: Doran N, Wade NE, Courtney KE, Sullivan RM, Jacobus J

primary_models.name: GEE longitudinal logistic regression of any alcohol, nicotine/tobacco, and cannabis use (4 timepoints) on age 11-12 phone ownership or social media use, adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, income, and time
primary_models.location_in_paper: Results pp. 3-4: phone x alcohol in Table 2 (p. 4); SM x alcohol in Table 3 (p. 5); phone x nicotine/tobacco in Supplementary Table 1, phone x cannabis in Supplementary Table 'S' (sic), SM x nicotine/tobacco in Supplementary Table 3, SM x cannabis in Supplementary Table 4 (supplement not bundled in PDF; values taken from Results text p. 3). Interpreted in Discussion pp. 4-6 and Abstract.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Predictor (phone ownership or social media use) and covariates measured once at the ABCD Year 2 annual visit (age 11-12, analytic baseline, time = 0) and treated as time-invariant. Outcome (any use of the substance since the prior assessment, binary) is time-varying across four assessments: Year 2 annual (time 0), Year 2 mid-year (1), Year 3 annual (2), Year 3 mid-year (3), roughly ages 11-12 to 13-14, data collected September 2018 to January 2022. Outcomes enter as repeated measures, not averaged. Six separate models, one per predictor x substance combination. Each model initially included predictor, linear time, and predictor x time; the interaction was dropped when non-significant. It was retained (significant) only for SM x alcohol and SM x nicotine/tobacco, so in those two models the SM main effect is the group difference at time 0 (age 11-12) and the interaction is the per-timepoint change in that log-odds difference. In the other four models the predictor main effect is the average group difference across all four timepoints.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (release not stated); all participants with substance use data at one or more of the four assessments, n = 10,907 (from the 11,880 enrolled). No imputation; all observed data used ('intent-to-treat'). Table 1 (age 11-12): mean age 12.0 years (SD 0.67); 52.5% male; 53.5% non-Hispanic white, 19.7% Hispanic or Latino, 14.2% Black or African American, 10.5% other; household income 11.1% < $25,000, 36.3% $25,000-$99,999, 31.1% $100,000-$200,000; grade 13.7% 5th, 44.2% 6th, 35.4% 7th; 67.8% of parents married. Per-model analytic N not reported.
primary_models.iv: Two binary predictors, each from a single youth-report item at the age 11-12 (Year 2) annual visit, modeled in separate models: (1) mobile phone ownership, 'Do you have your own mobile phone?' (0 = no, 1 = yes), endorsed by 71.2%; (2) social media use, 'Do you have at least one social media account?' (0 = no, 1 = yes), endorsed by 54.9%. The two overlap strongly (chi-square(1) = 1531.05, p < 0.001; 66.7% of phone owners vs 25.7% of non-owners used SM). Phone/SM is the IV.
primary_models.dv: Three binary time-varying outcomes, each modeled separately: any alcohol use, any nicotine/tobacco use, any cannabis use since the prior assessment. At annual visits (ages 11-12, 12-13) from the interviewer-assisted Timeline Followback; at the two mid-year phone assessments from a brief past-6-month substance use questionnaire. Prevalence at age 11-12 (Table 1): alcohol 9.9%, nicotine/tobacco 0.9%, cannabis 0.5%.

covariates.name: Age
covariates.detail: Years at the age 11-12 assessment, continuous, time-invariant

covariates.name: Racial/ethnic background
covariates.detail: Five categories (Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Asian, non-Hispanic white, Other); non-Hispanic white reference, 4 dummies

covariates.name: Household income
covariates.detail: Ordinal 1-10, higher = higher income, measured at ABCD baseline

covariates.name: Predictor x time
covariates.detail: Retained only in SM x alcohol and SM x nicotine/tobacco models; dropped elsewhere as non-significant

primary_models.equation: logit(P(SubUse[i,t] = 1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneOrSM[i] + b2*time[t] + b3*age[i] + b4*female[i] + b5*Black[i] + b6*Hispanic[i] + b7*Asian[i] + b8*Other[i] + b9*income[i] (+ b10*PhoneOrSM[i]*time[t] in the SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco models only); t = 0..3; within-person correlation handled by AR working correlation in GEE.
primary_models.estimation: Generalized estimating equations (Liang & Zeger 1986), Stata 17.0 xtgee, binomial family, logit link, autoregressive working correlation structure. No site or family clustering terms, no weights, no imputation. Alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Non-significant predictor x time interactions dropped; significant ones followed by simple-effects tests of time within each predictor level. Post-hoc sensitivity analysis refitting all models in substance-naive youth is extracted separately as M2. No sex, race, or other effect-modification tests reported.

primary_models.name: GEE longitudinal logistic regression of substance use on age 11-12 phone ownership or social media use in substance-naive youth (post-hoc sensitivity)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses', pp. 3-4 (text only, no table); summarized p. 4 and interpreted in Discussion p. 6 ('results of our post-hoc sensitivity analyses do suggest...').
primary_models.design: Same longitudinal design as M1 (predictor at age 11-12, binary substance use outcomes across four timepoints, time 0-3), refit in a subsample that was substance-naive at age 11-12 to address confounding by prior use. Predictor x time interaction tested and not significant in all six models, so dropped; predictor estimates are averaged group differences across the follow-up.
primary_models.sample: Subsample of M1 who reported at age 11-12 never having had more than a sip of alcohol and never having tried nicotine/tobacco or cannabis: n = 9,628 (87% of the original sample). No further demographics reported.
primary_models.iv: Same as M1: binary phone ownership and binary social media use (>= 1 account) at age 11-12, separate models.
primary_models.dv: Same as M1: any alcohol, any nicotine/tobacco, any cannabis use, time-varying binary across four assessments.

covariates.name: Time
covariates.detail: Linear 0-3; main effect reported in each model

covariates.name: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, household income
covariates.detail: Text says the models were 're-fit'; presumably the same covariates as M1, not explicitly restated

primary_models.equation: logit(P(SubUse[i,t] = 1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneOrSM[i] + b2*time[t] + covariates (as M1); no predictor x time term (non-significant in all six models).
primary_models.estimation: As M1: GEE, Stata 17.0 xtgee, binomial/logit, autoregressive working correlation, alpha = 0.05, no multiple-comparison correction. Post-hoc analysis.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000); CI endpoints converted the same way.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Binary contrast: phone owner vs non-owner, or has >= 1 social media account vs none, at age 11-12. For sm_x_time rows, the per-timepoint (about 6-month) change in the SM log-odds difference.
d_transformation.notes: OR converts directly via Chinn; no SDs needed. p0 values in M1 dv_axis are the marginal age 11-12 prevalences from Table 1 (p. 3), not the unexposed-group rate, and are not needed for the OR conversion. Caveats: (1) In M1 SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco, the SM OR is the difference at time 0 with an interaction retained, so it is not comparable to averaged effects in the other cells. (2) The SM-alcohol main effect in Table 3 (OR 1.50) conflicts with the Results text (OR 1.06, non-significant). (3) The sm_x_time interaction ORs are not a group contrast and probably should not be converted to d alongside the main effects. (4) Five of the six M1 models come from supplementary tables not included in the PDF; values were copied from the Results text.

extraction_flags: 1) The values for social media and alcohol disagree within the paper. Table 3 gives the SM main effect as OR 1.50 (1.31, 1.72), b 0.41. The Results text on p. 3 gives OR 1.06 [0.92, 1.21], b 0.04, not significant. The draft uses the table value, so a human needs to decide which is correct. 2) The supplementary tables (Supp Tables 1, 3, 4 and the one printed as 'S') are not in the PDF. Five of the six full-sample models were therefore copied from the Results text, and their p-values and SEs are missing. 3) In the SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco models the SM x time interaction was kept. That makes the SM main effect the difference at time 0, not an average over follow-up. The two interaction ORs are entered as a separate 'sm_x_time' IV row and probably should not be converted to d alongside the main effects. 4) M2 is the post-hoc sensitivity analysis in substance-naive youth (n=9,628). It is reported in the text only, but the authors interpret it in the Discussion. Its covariates are assumed to match M1 because the text only says the models were 're-fit'. 5) For phone and alcohol, p was entered as 0.001 with the label '<0.001'. The p0 values are the marginal age 11-12 prevalences from Table 1, not the rates in the unexposed group. 6) There are typos in the source: the CI '[1.01, 1.017]' for the SM x time OR, and '[0.06. 0.37]'. 7) The ABCD release is not stated, and per-model analytic N is not reported; only the total of 10,907 is given.
